newsitem.title: USA: White House sees U.S. expansion rolling on.
newsitem.headline: White House sees U.S. expansion rolling on.

text.p: The U.S. economy's nearly six-year expansion shows no signs of slowing down, with the country well placed to enjoy continued low unemployment and low inflation, the White House said on Monday.
The annual "Economic Report of the President," prepared by President Bill Clinton's Council of Economic Advisers, offered an optimistic vision of the economy.
"Our economy is stronger than it has been in decades," Clinton said in the report's opening paragraph, setting a tone reflected in many of the 424 pages of text and tables.

Predictions of economic trends have great political import in the United States, because such calculations underly the federal budget proposals that are subject to annual haggling between the Democratic president and Republican-led Congress.

The White House report found none of the classic signs that a downturn is around the corner -- financial imbalances, rising inflation, surplus inventories building up. And it argued that, unlike in years past, the United States can keep enjoying low rates of unemployment without rising inflation.

Council chairman Joseph Stiglitz, without directly commenting on the current sky-high level of the U.S. stock market, suggested that financial markets reflect the fundamental health of the U.S. economy.

"Overall, there is some degree of rational exuberance about our economy," Stiglitz told reporters in releasing the report. "Profits have been very, very high, the underlying fundamentals of the economy are very, very strong, interest rates are low.
"Those factors are consistent with a strong market."

In speaking of "rational exuberance," Stiglitz was playing on Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan's suggestion in December that there may be some "irrational exuberance" in the financial markets.
Greenspan's statement briefly knocked the stock market lower, but it has since resumed its climb and hit a string of record highs in January.
Although the White House report itself also avoids comment on the market, it made no bones about arguing that the economy appears poised to go on growing.
"Most recent expansions have ended because of rising inflation, financial imbalances or inventory overhangs," it said. "None of these conditions exists at present."

The report said household finances are sound, business inventories are lean and inflation remains under control, adding "the ability of the economy to sustain low unemployment and low inflation is the best it has been in years."

The report repeated the economic forecasts in Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget released on Thursday, calling for real gross domestic product growth of 2.0 percent this year and next, rising to 2.3 percent for the following five years.
It also forecast an unemployment rate of 5.3 percent in 1997, rising a touch to 5.5 percent in 1998. In January, the rate edged up to 5.4 percent from 5.3 percent in December.

"The administration does not think that 2.3 percent real growth in the long term is the best the United States can do," the report added, saying this pace reflected a conservative estimate. "The outcome could be even better."
